culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
Spain has diverse climate zones across different regions:

• Mediterranean Coast (Barcelona, Valencia): Hot, dry summers 25–32°C (77–90°F), mild winters 8–15°C (46–59°F). Peak tourist season June–September, but pleasant year-round

• Central Spain (Madrid, Toledo): Continental climate with hot, dry summers 30–40°C (86–104°F), cold winters 0–10°C (32–50°F). Significant day-night temperature variations. Spring (Apr–Jun) and fall (Sep–Oct) offer most comfortable temperatures

• Northern Spain (Bilbao, Santiago de Compostela): Atlantic climate with moderate temperatures 15–25°C (59–77°F) in summer, 5–15°C (41–59°F) in winter. More rainfall than other regions, especially in fall and winter

• Southern Spain (Seville, Málaga): Very hot, dry summers 35–45°C (95–113°F), mild winters 10–18°C (50–64°F). Best visited in spring or fall to avoid extreme heat

• Balearic Islands (Mallorca, Ibiza): Classic Mediterranean climate, slightly milder than mainland coast. Beach season May–October

• Canary Islands: Subtropical climate with warm temperatures 20–28°C (68–82°F) year-round, making them an excellent winter beach destination

• Most of Spain experiences high UV index—sun protection is essential year-round

currencyInfo.name: Euro
currencyInfo.tips:
• ATMs widely available in cities and towns

• Credit cards accepted at most establishments (Visa/Mastercard more widely accepted than American Express)

• Inform your bank of travel plans to prevent card blocks

• Tipping is not obligatory but appreciated: 5–10% in restaurants for good service, 1–2€ for hotel porters, round up taxi fares to nearest euro

• Always have some cash for small shops, markets, and cafés in rural areas

• Many smaller establishments don't accept bills larger than 50€

• VAT (IVA) of 21% included in displayed prices

• Non-EU residents can request tax refunds on purchases over 90.16€ at participating stores (look for "Tax Free" signs)

• Spain generally has lower prices than northern European countries but higher than eastern Europe

localCustoms.title: Greeting Style
localCustoms.description: Spaniards typically greet with two kisses on the cheeks between women or a woman and man. Men usually shake hands. When entering small shops, saying "Hola" is polite. First names are used quickly, but professional titles (Doctor, Professor) are important in formal settings.

localCustoms.title: Dining Customs
localCustoms.description: Spanish mealtimes are later than in America: lunch (la comida) 2-4pm, dinner (la cena) 9-11pm. The midday meal is typically the largest. Tapas culture involves sharing small plates. Leaving a small amount of food shows you're satisfied. Service is included but small tips (5-10%) are appreciated for good service.

localCustoms.title: Siesta Tradition
localCustoms.description: Though less common in major cities, smaller towns still observe siesta hours (roughly 2-5pm) when smaller shops close. Plan accordingly. Many businesses have long workdays with a substantial break in the middle. Museums and major attractions usually remain open throughout the day.

localCustoms.title: Public Behavior
localCustoms.description: Spaniards are expressive and animated in conversation—interrupting is often a sign of engagement, not rudeness. Public spaces are lively, and quietness can be perceived as unfriendly. Volume levels, especially in restaurants, are higher than Americans might expect.

localCustoms.title: Regional Identities
localCustoms.description: Spain has strong regional cultures and languages. In Catalonia, the Basque Country, and Galicia, locals appreciate visitors recognizing their distinct identity and a few words in their language (Catalan, Euskera, Galician). Avoid referring to everything as "Spanish" in these regions.

localCustoms.title: Nightlife Timing
localCustoms.description: Spanish nightlife starts late—locals rarely go out before 11pm, and clubs don't fill until after 1am, with peak hours between 2-5am. Pacing yourself is essential. Pre-gaming often includes bar-hopping for tapas (tapeo) before clubbing begins.

localCustoms.title: Personal Space
localCustoms.description: Personal space boundaries are closer than in America. Standing close during conversation is normal. Public transportation and elevators will feel more crowded. Queues (lines) may appear disorganized but have their own logic—ask "¿Quién es el último?" (Who's last?) to find your place.

localCustoms.title: Religious Observances
localCustoms.description: Despite increasing secularism, Catholic traditions remain important. During Holy Week (Semana Santa) and local patron saint festivals, expect processions, modified business hours, and increased accommodation prices. Respect religious ceremonies by dressing modestly and maintaining appropriate behavior.

culturalTaboos.title: Discussing politics, especially regional independence movements, unless invited
Being excessively loud in non
Expecting quick service in restaurants
Bare feet in public places other than beaches
Assuming all of Spain enjoys bullfighting (it's controversial in many regions)
Discussing money or asking personal financial questions
Failing to greet shop owners upon entering small businesses
Excessive public drunkenness
Rushing or showing impatience with a more relaxed pace of life
Comparing Spanish cuisine unfavorably to other Mediterranean cuisines

safetyTips.title: Pickpocket Awareness
safetyTips.description: Barcelona, Madrid, and other tourist areas have skilled pickpockets. Use anti-theft bags, keep valuables secured, and be especially vigilant in crowded areas, public transportation, and popular attractions. Beware of distraction techniques like spilling something on you or asking for directions.

safetyTips.title: Beach Safety
safetyTips.description: Pay attention to beach flags: Green (safe), Yellow (caution), and Red (dangerous). The Mediterranean can have sudden drop-offs and occasional strong currents. Leave valuables at your accommodation or use locker services. Apply sunscreen regularly—the Spanish sun is stronger than it feels.

safetyTips.title: Road Safety
safetyTips.description: Spain has excellent highways (autopistas) but rural roads can be narrow and winding. Mountain driving requires experience. Zero alcohol tolerance for new drivers. Always carry required documents (license, insurance, registration). Speed cameras are common, and fines are substantial.

safetyTips.title: Night Safety
safetyTips.description: Most Spanish cities are relatively safe at night, but take normal precautions. Use licensed taxis or ride-sharing apps after midnight. In Madrid and Barcelona, be cautious in areas like Raval or Lavapiés late at night. Women should be aware that solo bar-hopping may invite unwanted attention.

safetyTips.title: Heat Precautions
safetyTips.description: Summer temperatures regularly exceed 38°C (100°F), especially in southern Spain. Heat stroke is a real risk. Stay hydrated, seek shade during peak hours (12-4pm), and consider scheduling indoor activities during the hottest part of the day. Air conditioning is not universal in older buildings.

safetyTips.title: Emergency Services
safetyTips.description: The general emergency number is 112 (equivalent to 911). For police only, call 091. Spain has excellent public healthcare, but travel insurance is recommended. Pharmacies (farmacias) are marked with a green cross and can provide basic medical advice for minor issues.

commonScams.title: Petition Scams
commonScams.description: People (often appearing to be deaf or disabled) approach with clipboards asking you to sign petitions for fake charities, then demand money or pickpocket you while you're distracted. Politely decline to engage and keep walking.

commonScams.title: Friendship Bracelet Trick
commonScams.description: Common near tourist sites, someone offers to tie a "friendship bracelet" on your wrist, then demands payment. Once tied, it's difficult to remove without paying. Firmly refuse these "gifts" and keep your hands close to your body when approached.

commonScams.title: Restaurant Tourist Menus
commonScams.description: Some restaurants in highly touristic areas offer overpriced "tourist menus" with mediocre food. Restaurants with menu boards only in English or with staff actively recruiting from the sidewalk often fall into this category. Look for places where locals eat, typically a block or two away from main attractions.

commonScams.title: Fake Police Officers
commonScams.description: Scammers posing as plainclothes police may ask to check your wallet for counterfeit bills or ID. Real Spanish police rarely ask to see wallets. Request to go to the nearest police station to show documents, or ask for their police ID first (all officers must carry one).

commonScams.title: La Flamenquería
commonScams.description: Tourist traps advertising "authentic flamenco" often offer poor-quality shows at high prices. Research reputable venues in advance—authentic performances are rarely heavily advertised on the street. In Andalucía, look for "peñas flamencas" for more authentic experiences.

interestingFacts: Second most spoken native language in the world.
Regional languages like Catalan, Basque, and Galician also hold official status.

culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
France has varied climates across different regions:

• Paris & Northern France: Spring (Mar–May): Cool 10–18°C (50–64°F), frequent showers

• Summer (Jun–Aug): Warm 15–25°C (59–77°F), occasional heat waves 30–35°C (86–95°F)

• Autumn (Sep–Nov): Mild 10–18°C (50–64°F), increasing rain

• Winter (Dec–Feb): Cold 1–7°C (34–45°F), occasional freezing temperatures

• Southern France: Mediterranean climate, 5–10°C (41–50°F) warmer than north year-round

• Alpine regions: Much colder in winter −5 to 0°C (23–32°F), cool summers 10–20°C (50–68°F)

• Currency exchange booths often have poor rates—ATMs better

localCustoms.title: Greeting Etiquette
localCustoms.description: Shake hands when meeting someone for the first time. "La bise" (cheek kisses) is for friends and family. Begin conversations with "Bonjour" (or "Bonsoir" in evening) before asking questions.

localCustoms.title: Dining Protocol
localCustoms.description: Keep hands visible on table, not in lap. Bread placed directly on tablecloth. Wait for "bon appétit" before eating. Finish everything on your plate. Tipping optional (5-10% for excellent service).

localCustoms.title: Shopping Courtesy
localCustoms.description: Greet shopkeepers with "Bonjour" when entering and "Au revoir" when leaving. Ask permission before touching items in small shops. Many stores close on Sundays and for lunch (12-2pm).

localCustoms.title: Language Respect
localCustoms.description: Attempt a few French phrases before switching to English. Begin with "Parlez-vous anglais?" (Do you speak English?). Even basic French efforts are appreciated and will improve your experience.

localCustoms.title: Personal Space
localCustoms.description: The French value personal privacy. Avoid personal questions about job, income, or marital status with new acquaintances. Keep your voice down in public spaces.

localCustoms.title: Punctuality
localCustoms.description: Arrive 5-10 minutes late for dinner invitations at homes, but be on time for restaurants and business meetings. Museum entrance times on tickets are often strictly enforced.

localCustoms.title: Dress Code
localCustoms.description: Dress smartly in cities, especially Paris. Avoid athletic wear, shorts, and flip-flops in urban areas unless exercising. Shoulders and knees should be covered when visiting religious sites.

localCustoms.title: Public Behavior
localCustoms.description: Public displays of affection are common but keep it tasteful. Public intoxication is frowned upon. Maintain composure and avoid loud conversations in public transportation.

culturalTaboos.title: Addressing people by first name without invitation
Discussing money, salary, or personal questions with new acquaintances
Loud talking in restaurants or public transportation
Snapping fingers to get service in restaurants or shops
Chewing gum in public, especially in formal settings
Asking "What do you do?" early in conversation
Bringing wine to a dinner party without asking (host selects wine carefully)
Walking into shops without greeting staff
Rushing through meals
Being overly friendly with strangers

safetyTips.title: Pickpocketing
safetyTips.description: Common in tourist areas, particularly Paris metro, Eiffel Tower, and Montmartre. Use anti-theft bags, keep valuables in front pockets or hidden pouches. Be extra vigilant in crowded areas.

safetyTips.title: Tourist Scams
safetyTips.description: Beware of petition signers, friendship bracelet offers, or gold ring scams. Official ticket sellers never sell on streets. Ignore anyone claiming to have "found" jewelry or asking if you "dropped" something.

safetyTips.title: Transportation Safety
safetyTips.description: Use official taxis or ride-sharing apps. In Paris, metro stations can be unsafe late at night—consider using buses after hours. Driving requires adjustment to local rules and roundabouts.

safetyTips.title: Beach Safety
safetyTips.description: Mediterranean beaches may have strong currents. Obey flag warnings. Red flag means no swimming allowed, yellow means caution, green means safe conditions. Topless sunbathing is acceptable on many beaches.

safetyTips.title: Emergency Preparedness
safetyTips.description: France has experienced terrorist incidents. Stay alert in public spaces. Follow authorities' instructions during any incident. Register with your embassy for emergency alerts.

safetyTips.title: Protests
safetyTips.description: Demonstrations are common, particularly in Paris. These can turn disruptive with little warning. Avoid areas where protests are occurring, even if they appear peaceful initially.

commonScams.title: Petition Scams
commonScams.description: People with clipboards ask you to sign petitions, then demand money or pickpocket you while distracted. Firmly say "Non, merci" and walk away.

commonScams.title: Friendship Bracelet
commonScams.description: Common at Sacré-Cœur in Paris—someone ties string around your finger/wrist, creates a "bracelet," then demands payment. Refuse firmly and keep walking.

commonScams.title: Restaurant Overcharging
commonScams.description: Always check if service (15%) is included. Review bill for items you didn't order. Tourist restaurants near attractions may have inflated prices—check menu before sitting.

commonScams.title: Taxi Scams
commonScams.description: Unofficial taxis may take longer routes or charge excessive rates. Use official taxis (with illuminated signs) or ride-sharing apps. Airport to Paris has fixed rates—know them in advance.

commonScams.title: Gold Ring Trick
commonScams.description: Someone "finds" a gold ring near you, asks if it's yours, then offers to sell it cheaply. The ring is worthless brass. Say "Non" and continue walking.

interestingFacts: Known as the language of diplomacy and culinary arts.

culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
Italy has varied climates from north to south:

• Spring (Mar–May): Mild 10–20°C (50–68°F), occasional rain

• Summer (Jun–Aug): Hot 25–35°C (77–95°F), very hot in south 30–40°C (86–104°F)

• Autumn (Sep–Nov): Pleasant 15–25°C (59–77°F), rainier in north

• Winter (Dec–Feb): Cold in north 0–10°C (32–50°F), milder in south 10–15°C (50–59°F)

• Alps: Winter snow, below freezing −5–0°C (23–32°F)

• Sicily/Sardinia: Mild winters 10–15°C (50–59°F), hot summers 30–35°C (86–95°F)

items: Prescription medications in original packaging
Sunscreen (especially in summer)
Insect repellent (for rural areas and summer evenings)
Basic first-aid supplies
Hand sanitizer and wet wipes
Motion sickness remedies for boat rides and winding roads
Pain relievers and digestive aids
Lip balm with SPF

essentialItems.title: Outdoor Gear
items: Daypack for sightseeing
Reusable water bottle (tap water is generally safe)
Travel umbrella

localCustoms.title: Dining Etiquette
localCustoms.description: Eat dinner later (7:30–9:00pm). Keep hands visible on table, not in lap. Don't rush meals—they're social events.

localCustoms.title: Greetings
localCustoms.description: Double cheek kisses are common between friends (left cheek first). Handshakes for business settings.

localCustoms.title: Dress Code
localCustoms.description: Italians dress well even for casual outings. Avoid sportswear in cities. Cover shoulders and knees when visiting churches.

localCustoms.title: Riposo (Afternoon Break)
localCustoms.description: Many shops close from roughly 1:00–4:00pm, especially in smaller towns. Plan your shopping accordingly.

localCustoms.title: Coffee Culture
localCustoms.description: Drink cappuccino only before 11:00am. Order at the register first, then take receipt to the bar. Standing at the bar costs less than table service.

localCustoms.title: Personal Space
localCustoms.description: Italians stand closer when conversing than many northern Europeans or Americans. Stepping back might be perceived as coldness.

localCustoms.title: Tipping
localCustoms.description: Service (servizio) is often included. If not, 5–10% is appreciated but not expected. Round up taxi fares.

localCustoms.title: Volume
localCustoms.description: Animated conversations are normal. Talking loudly isn't considered rude in many social settings.

culturalTaboos.title: Touching produce at markets without asking (let vendors select for you)
Eating on the go in formal settings
Requesting cheese on seafood pasta dishes
Ordering cappuccino with or after dinner
Speaking loudly inside churches or museums
Wearing revealing clothing in religious sites
Being overly rigid about schedules and timing
Eating bread before the main course arrives
Requesting substitutions at traditional restaurants
Declining offered food or drink in someone's home

safetyTips.title: Pickpocketing
safetyTips.description: Common in tourist areas of Rome, Florence, Naples, and on public transport. Use anti-theft bags and keep valuables secure.

safetyTips.title: Tourist Scams
safetyTips.description: Be wary of "friendship bracelet" offers, fake petitions, or distraction techniques. Always verify prices before ordering at restaurants.

safetyTips.title: Traffic Safety
safetyTips.description: Driving can be aggressive in cities. Pedestrians should use crosswalks and be alert—cars may not always stop.

safetyTips.title: Evening Safety
safetyTips.description: Train stations and their surroundings can be sketchy at night. Take official taxis after dark.

safetyTips.title: Natural Hazards
safetyTips.description: Italy has seismic activity. Follow local guidance during earthquakes. Summer wildfires can occur in dry regions.

safetyTips.title: Beach Safety
safetyTips.description: Respect flag warnings at beaches. Red flags mean dangerous conditions. Be cautious of strong currents and underwater rocks.

commonScams.title: Unofficial Guides
commonScams.description: Only use licensed guides with official badges. Unauthorized guides may overcharge or provide inaccurate information.

commonScams.title: Taxi Overcharging
commonScams.description: Use official taxis (white with meters) and confirm approximate fare before departing. Some drivers take longer routes for tourists.

commonScams.title: Restaurant Tricks
commonScams.description: Check if bread and water are free before consuming. Review bill carefully for unexpected "coperto" (cover charge) or service fees.

commonScams.title: Designer Knockoffs
commonScams.description: Buying counterfeit goods is illegal and can result in hefty fines. Street vendors selling designer items are selling fakes.

commonScams.title: Helpful "Strangers"
commonScams.description: Be suspicious of overly helpful strangers at train ticket machines who may be trying to confuse you and steal your money or credit card.

interestingFacts: Hand gestures are famously integral to everyday spoken expression.

culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
Italy has varied climates from north to south:

• Spring (Mar–May): Mild 10–20°C (50–68°F), occasional rain

• Summer (Jun–Aug): Hot 25–35°C (77–95°F), very hot in south 30–40°C (86–104°F)

• Autumn (Sep–Nov): Pleasant 15–25°C (59–77°F), rainier in north

• Winter (Dec–Feb): Cold in north 0–10°C (32–50°F), milder in south 10–15°C (50–59°F)

• Alps: Winter snow, below freezing −5–0°C (23–32°F)

• Sicily/Sardinia: Mild winters 10–15°C (50–59°F), hot summers 30–35°C (86–95°F)

currencyInfo.name: Euro
currencyInfo.tips:
• ATMs widely available in cities and towns

• Many smaller establishments prefer cash

• Credit cards accepted at most hotels and larger restaurants

• Notify your bank of travel plans to avoid card blocks

• Keep small cash denominations for cafés and small purchases

• Service charge often included; small tips appreciated

• Currency exchange offices charge high fees—better to use ATMs

culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
Varied Mediterranean & continental climate:
• Spring (Apr–May): 15–23°C, pleasant blooms
• Summer (Jun–Aug): Hot & dry, 28–35°C (82–95°F)
• Autumn (Sep–Oct): Warm sea & mild cities, 18–26°C
• Winter (Nov–Feb): Chilly 5–12°C with rain in Istanbul, snow in Cappadocia

currencyInfo.name: Turkish Lira
currencyInfo.tips:
• Cash is needed for small shops, public restrooms, taxis, and bazaars
• Pay by credit card for hotels and major restaurants to get official bank rates
• Tipping 10% in cash directly to waitstaff is appreciated in restaurants

essentialItems.title: Modesty & Exploration
items: Modest attire covering shoulders, knees, and chest for visiting mosques (Blue Mosque, Hagia Sophia)
Lightweight headscarf or pashmina for women when entering functioning mosques
Easy slip-on walking shoes (shoes must be removed and placed in plastic bags at mosque entrances)
Sturdy flat walking shoes with excellent tread for steep, slick cobblestone streets (Galata, Sultanahmet)
Breathable linen clothing for summer heat, or warm windproof coat for winter along the Bosphorus
Polarized sunglasses and high-SPF sun protection

essentialItems.title: Electronics & Power
items: Type C / F European two-pin round plug adapter (standard 230V, 50Hz)
Istanbulkart transit app or reloadable transit card for Bosphorus ferries, trams, and metro
BiTaksi app for licensed, metered yellow and turquoise taxi dispatch
High-capacity portable battery pack for all-day photography and map lookups
Turkish travel eSIM for dependable mobile data across cities and coastlines

essentialItems.title: Documents, Currency & Health
items: Physical passport valid for at least 6 months from entry date with blank pages for entry/exit stamps
Turkish Lira (TRY) cash reserve in small banknotes for bazaars, street vendors, tips, and public restrooms
Credit or debit card with 0% foreign transaction fees
Comprehensive travel health insurance policy document
Personal medications, motion sickness pills for ferry rides, and probiotic stomach remedies

localCustoms.title: Hospitality & Tea (Çay)
localCustoms.description: Accepting a small tulip glass of hot Turkish tea is a gesture of friendship and warmth. It is often offered for free in carpet shops and bazaars.

localCustoms.title: Shoe Removal in Mosques & Homes
localCustoms.description: Always remove shoes before stepping onto carpets in mosques and Turkish homes.

culturalTaboos.title: Disrespecting Atatürk or the Flag
culturalTaboos.description: Insulting the Turkish Republic, its founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, or defacing the flag is strictly illegal.

safetyTips.title: Taxi Meter Enforcement
safetyTips.description: Always verify the driver turns on the digital meter in the rearview mirror ('Taksimetre açar mısınız?').

commonScams.title: Shoe Shine Brush Drop
commonScams.description: A shoe shiner walking ahead 'accidentally' drops his brush. If you pick it up, he will offer a free thank-you shine and then aggressively demand $10–$20.

commonScams.title: Befriending for Nightclub Drinks
commonScams.description: Strangers around Taksim inviting you to a club where you are trapped with a massive bill.

interestingFacts: An agglutinative language featuring vowel harmony.
Uses a modified Latin alphabet introduced in 1928.

culturalInfo.weatherInfo:
Japan has four distinct seasons:
• Spring (Mar–May): Cherry blossoms, mild 10–20°C (50–68°F)
• Summer (Jun–Aug): Rainy season in June, humid 25–35°C (77–95°F), typhoons Aug–Sep
• Autumn (Sep–Nov): Comfortable 15–25°C (59–77°F), vibrant foliage
• Winter (Dec–Feb): Snow in the north (Hokkaido –10 to 0°C), milder in Tokyo 5–10°C (41–50°F)

currencyInfo.name: Japanese Yen
currencyInfo.tips:
• Cash remains widely used—carry sufficient yen bills
• ATMs at 7-Eleven, Japan Post & major convenience stores accept foreign cards
• Use Suica/Pasmo/IC cards for subways, buses & vending machines
• Strictly no tipping culture—it can cause confusion or be considered impolite
• Exchange currency at airports or major bank counters

emergencyInfo.embassy: US Embassy Tokyo: +81 3-3224-5000 | UK Embassy Tokyo: +81 3-5275-3200

essentialItems.title: Clothing
items: Slip-on shoes (you will remove shoes frequently at shrines, ryokans & restaurants)
Comfortable walking shoes for 15,000+ daily steps
Layered clothing for varying indoor heating / air conditioning
Compact travel umbrella (or buy clear umbrella at konbini)
Modest clothing for visiting temples and shrines
Thermal base layers for winter trips

essentialItems.title: Electronics & Connectivity
items: Type A power adapter (two-prong flat, 100V, 50/60Hz)
High-capacity portable charger / power bank for navigating transit
eSIM or Pocket Wi-Fi device (essential for Tokyo train navigation)
Suica or Pasmo digital transit card loaded on Apple/Google Wallet
Google Maps & Google Translate with offline Japanese dictionary downloaded

essentialItems.title: Documents & Essentials
items: Passport (law requires tourists to carry physical passport at all times)
Visit Japan Web QR codes (fast-track customs & immigration)
Small coin purse (yen uses many high-value 100, 500 yen coins)
Small plastic bag or pouch for trash (public trash cans are rare)
Hand towel or handkerchief (many public restrooms lack paper towels)

localCustoms.title: Bowing Etiquette
localCustoms.description: Depth and duration of bows vary by context—from a subtle head nod to a respectful bow—used for greetings, gratitude, and apologies.

localCustoms.title: Shoe Removal (Genkan)
localCustoms.description: Always remove shoes indoors at homes, traditional ryokan, tatami seating, and temples. Slippers are provided, but remove them before stepping on tatami.

localCustoms.title: Train & Transit Etiquette
localCustoms.description: Keep phones on silent (Manner Mode). Avoid phone calls on trains. Speak in hushed tones and take your backpack off your back in crowded cars.

localCustoms.title: No Tipping Culture
localCustoms.description: Tipping does not exist in Japan and can create awkward situations. Great service is built into the culture and price.

culturalTaboos.title: Chopstick Mistakes
culturalTaboos.description: Never stick chopsticks vertically into a bowl of rice (resembles funeral incense) or pass food directly chopstick-to-chopstick.

culturalTaboos.title: Walking While Eating
culturalTaboos.description: Eating or drinking while walking down streets is considered impolite. Eat near the vending machine or store where purchased.

culturalTaboos.title: Tattoos in Onsen (Hot Springs)
culturalTaboos.description: Many traditional onsens forbid visible tattoos. Seek tattoo-friendly baths or private kashikiri ryokan baths.

safetyTips.title: One of the World's Safest Destinations
safetyTips.description: Violent crime is exceedingly rare. Lost items are routinely turned into Koban (police boxes) and recovered intact.

safetyTips.title: Earthquake Preparedness
safetyTips.description: Japan experiences regular seismic activity. Download the 'Safety Tips' app from the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO).

safetyTips.title: Pedestrian & Traffic Discipline
safetyTips.description: Follow pedestrian lights strictly even on quiet streets; cars drive on the left side of the road.

commonScams.title: Kabukicho / Roppongi Touts
commonScams.description: Do not follow nightlife touts offering 'cheap drinks' or free entry in nightlife districts; patrons may face exorbitant hidden cover fees.

commonScams.title: Fake Monks Soliciting Donations
commonScams.description: Near major tourist temples (e.g., Asakusa), fraudulent people dressed as monks may offer bracelets and demand immediate cash.

interestingFacts: Uses three writing scripts: Hiragana, Katakana, and Kanji.
Politeness and honorifics (keigo) are essential in social interactions.
